stem: The human eye can focus on objects at different distances by adjusting the focal length of the eye lens. This is due to
solution:
The ability of the eye to adjust the focal length of its lens and so focus on both near and distant objects is called **accommodation**.

The other three are defects, not abilities: presbyopia is the loss of accommodation with age, near-sightedness (myopia) is the inability to see distant objects clearly, and far-sightedness (hypermetropia) the inability to see near objects clearly.

stem: The human eye forms the image of an object at its
solution:
The image is formed on the **retina**, the light-sensitive screen at the back of the eyeball. Its light-sensitive cells generate electrical signals, which travel along the optic nerve to the brain.

The others are not screens: the **cornea** is the transparent front surface where most of the refraction occurs, the **iris** is the coloured muscular diaphragm, and the **pupil** is the opening in the iris through which light enters.
groundedIn: §10.1 The Human Eye — the structure of the eye and the role of the retina.

stem: The least distance of distinct vision for a young adult with normal vision is about
solution:
The least distance of distinct vision — the near point — is about **25 cm** for a young adult with normal vision. It is the closest an object can be brought and still be seen clearly without strain.

The other options are out by a factor of 10 or 100, which is exactly the trap: read the unit as carefully as the number.
groundedIn: §10.1.1 — 'For a young adult with normal vision, it is about 25 cm.'

stem: The change in focal length of an eye lens is caused by the action of the
solution:
The **ciliary muscles** change the curvature of the eye lens, and so its focal length. When they contract the lens thickens and the focal length shortens; when they relax the lens thins and the focal length lengthens.

The pupil and iris control only how much light enters, and the retina is the screen on which the image falls — none of the three alters the focal length.
groundedIn: §10.1.1 — 'the ciliary muscles change the curvature of the eye lens... the focal length of the eye lens changes'.

subtopic: Defects of Vision and their Correction
stem: A person needs a lens of power \(-5.5\) dioptres for correcting his distant vision. For correcting his near vision he needs a lens of power \(+1.5\) dioptre. What is the focal length of the lens required for correcting (i) distant vision, and (ii) near vision?
solution:
The power of a lens and its focal length are related by \(P = \dfrac{1}{f}\), with \(f\) in metres.

**(i) Distant vision.** \(P = -5.5\,\text{D}\)

\(f = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{-5.5} = -0.18\,\text{m}\)

The negative sign shows it is a **concave** lens, as expected for correcting myopia.

**(ii) Near vision.** \(P = +1.5\,\text{D}\)

\(f = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{1.5} = +0.67\,\text{m}\)

The positive sign shows it is a **convex** lens, as expected for correcting hypermetropia. A person needing both is prescribed bi-focal lenses.
groundedIn: §10.2 — the correction of myopia by a concave lens and hypermetropia by a convex lens, with bi-focal lenses for a person with both.

subtopic: Defects of Vision and their Correction
stem: The far point of a myopic person is 80 cm in front of the eye. What is the nature and power of the lens required to correct the problem?
solution:
To correct myopia the lens must form, at the person's own far point, the image of an object at infinity. So the image distance is the far-point distance, on the same side as the object:

\(v = -80\,\text{cm} = -0.8\,\text{m}\), \(u = \infty\)

Using the lens formula \(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{-0.8} - \dfrac{1}{\infty} = -1.25\)

\(f = -0.8\,\text{m}\)

**Nature: a concave (diverging) lens.**

**Power:** \(P = \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{-0.8} = -1.25\,\text{D}\)
groundedIn: §10.2 — myopia is corrected by a concave lens whose focal length equals the distance of the far point.

subtopic: Defects of Vision and their Correction
stem: Make a diagram to show how hypermetropia is corrected. The near point of a hypermetropic eye is 1 m. What is the power of the lens required to correct this defect? Assume that the near point of the normal eye is 25 cm.
solution:
**The diagram.** Draw three panels, as in the book's own figure for hypermetropia:

- the hypermetropic eye with an object at 25 cm, its rays converging to a point **behind** the retina;
- the same eye showing that it can only focus from its own near point at 1 m;
- the corrected eye, with a **convex lens** placed before it, bringing the image back onto the retina.

**The calculation.** The convex lens must take an object at the normal near point and form its image at the eye's own near point:

\(u = -25\,\text{cm} = -0.25\,\text{m}\), \(v = -100\,\text{cm} = -1\,\text{m}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{-1} - \dfrac{1}{-0.25} = -1 + 4 = 3\)

\(f = \dfrac{1}{3}\,\text{m} = +0.33\,\text{m}\)

\(P = \dfrac{1}{f} = +3.0\,\text{D}\)

So a **convex lens of power \(+3.0\,\text{D}\)** is required.
groundedIn: §10.2 — hypermetropia and its correction by a convex lens of suitable power, with the sign convention of the lens formula.

stem: Why is a normal eye not able to see clearly the objects placed closer than 25 cm?
solution:
To focus on a nearer object the eye must shorten the focal length of its lens, which it does by contracting the ciliary muscles so that the lens becomes thicker and more curved.

But the lens can only be curved so far. At about 25 cm the ciliary muscles have contracted as much as they can, and the focal length has reached its **minimum**. For an object closer than that, the required focal length is shorter still, and the eye simply cannot produce it — the image falls behind the retina and looks blurred.

Trying to look closer also strains the ciliary muscles, which is why 25 cm is described as the least distance of distinct vision *without strain*.
groundedIn: §10.1.1 — the limit of accommodation and the least distance of distinct vision.

stem: What happens to the image distance in the eye when we increase the distance of an object from the eye?
solution:
The image distance **does not change** — it stays fixed at the distance between the eye lens and the retina, because the image must always be formed on the retina for us to see clearly.

What changes instead is the **focal length of the eye lens**. As the object moves further away, the ciliary muscles relax, the lens becomes thinner and its focal length increases, keeping the image exactly on the retina.

This is the opposite of what happens with an ordinary camera or optical bench, where the focal length is fixed and the image distance moves.
groundedIn: §10.1 and §10.1.1 — the image is always formed on the retina, and accommodation works by changing the focal length rather than the image distance.

solution:
The twinkling of stars is caused by **atmospheric refraction** of starlight.

A star is so far away that it is effectively a point source. Its light passes through the earth's atmosphere, whose layers have continuously changing optical densities and are constantly in motion. The starlight is therefore refracted by a continuously varying amount, so it reaches the eye along a slightly different path from moment to moment.

Two things follow:

- the star's **apparent position keeps shifting** slightly;
- the **amount of light entering the eye keeps changing**, so the star looks bright at one moment and dim the next.

That flickering in brightness and position is what we see as twinkling.
groundedIn: §10.5 Atmospheric Refraction — the twinkling of stars due to the continuously changing atmosphere.

stem: Explain why the planets do not twinkle.
solution:
Planets are much **closer** to the earth than stars are, so a planet is not a point source — it can be regarded as a **collection of a very large number of point sources** spread over an extended area.

Each of those point sources twinkles, but they do not all brighten and dim together. The variations in the light coming from the different points **average out**, so the total amount of light entering the eye stays effectively constant.

With no change in brightness, a planet shines steadily and does not appear to twinkle.
groundedIn: §10.5 Atmospheric Refraction — planets are extended sources and 'the twinkling effects of the points nullify each other'.

stem: Why does the sky appear dark instead of blue to an astronaut?
solution:
The sky looks blue to us because the molecules of the **atmosphere scatter** sunlight, and blue light, having a shorter wavelength, is scattered much more strongly than red. That scattered blue light reaches our eyes from all directions, so the sky glows blue.

An astronaut is above the atmosphere, where there is effectively **no air and no scattering particles**. With nothing to scatter the sunlight sideways, no light reaches the astronaut's eyes except directly from the Sun and other objects.

So the sky appears **dark** instead of blue.
groundedIn: §10.6.2 Why is the colour of the clear Sky Blue? and §10.6 Scattering of Light.
